title: tRNA Therapy
body_text: Here’s an RNA-based therapeutic approach that’s well worth keeping an eye on, not least because it takes a different path than the ones that most of us have heard about. This transfer-RNA (tRNA) route would be directed at nonsense mutations that lead to human disease, and would be an alternative to gene therapy, or to the various “read-through” agents that have been attempted to try to transcribe past these premature-translation-codon (PTC) roadblocks. How does one do that? By provided “suppressor transfer RNAs” (sup-tRNAs), which is one of those ideas that is conceptually pretty straightforward but where the details have proven very hard to work through. For example, one way to get these things into a living organism is to use a viral vector (like AAV) to insert the sequences for them into the host’s genome, which is in effect just a variation on direct gene therapy. That comes with all the disadvantages thereof, such as how durable the expression ends up being, how immunogenic the AAV vector is in actual patients, and the likelihood that any such immune response could make it impossible to ever dose such a patient with an AAV vector again, either to “top up” this route or for any other therapeutic reason. (There's also been a report of an interesting approach that combines sup-tRNA technology with gene editing) People have also tried delivering such sup-tRNA species directly through lipid nanoparticles, the route that has proven quite effective in RNA-based vaccines. But these are pretty large and complex sequences, and up until now these attempts have not really made much of a therapeutic difference due to low efficacy and pharmacokinetic problems. The LNP delivery ideas can be very powerful, but I think it’s safe to say that we have a lot to learn about them and that there are many possible variations that just haven’t been studied yet. This new paper has promising data in that area, though. It uses nonsense mutations in the CFTR gene that cause cystic fibrosis as a proving ground, and that’s a very clear-cut case, although not an easy one. That’s because it’s easiest to deliver LNP cargoes straight into the liver - that’s where they’re going to end up anyway, for the most part - but for CF you would like then to hit the lung membranes instead. It would be a real advance to do so, though, because there are CF patients with such nonsense mutations that don’t respond well to the existing CFTR drug combos that have been so transformative for other mutations in that protein. The team reports a number of modifications on the RNA species itself, reminiscent of the modifications that were found to greatly increase the effectiveness of the RNA vaccine sequences. Trying a whole range of these out in various structural regions of the tRNA molecules and running them through reporter-gene cell assays (which were engineered to show luciferase activity if successful read-through was achieved) showed a whole range of effects, with some increases and some notable decreases as well. Combining these often worked, although in an additive (as opposed to synergistic) fashion, and they were further evaluated for their immunogenic potential. Further studies revealed the effect of these changes on the key aminoacylation step where tRNAs are charged with the correct amino acid(s) for delivery. A particular mutations (m1-A58) really stood out here as an improvement, and this change also extended the lifetime of the read-through effects i the cell assays as well. These effects were confirmed in a transgenic luciferase-reporter mouse model, and at this point the team went on to try to optimize the LNP formulations for better pulmonary tissue delivery. Screening a thousand new ionizable lipid species across a range of structures and various RNA types showed that the landscape was complicated: the best lipid designs varied a lot depending on what RNA modality and cargo was being used. So there is (well as of yet) no substitute for tuning this up on your particular RNA idea; taking some off-the-shelf (or off-the literature) recipe is probably not a good way forward. The work went forward with a model that tried to mimic the thick-mucus-coating conditions that are found in actual CF-diseased lungs, and identified a particular lipid formulation that stood out (which, as you’d guess from the above, was nothing like you’d have picked based on mRNA LNP formulation precedent). The next model used a fluorescent aptamer-based species to track where the RNA species were delivered in rodents and how long they persisted, and these helped confirm that the desired airway cells could indeed be targeted. When the optimized system was charged with candidate tRNA species and these were tried on cells expressing nonsense CFTR mutations (G542X), the team found that the tRNAs delivering the desired glycine were only moderately effective. The sup-tRNA delivering arginine, though, was better, and it had already been determined that the arginine mutation at this position led to a functional CFTR, so they went with that. A known mutation that needed an arginine anyway (R1162X) was also treated successfully. Minimal off-target effects were found. Dosing these in mice (intratracheal administration) also showed no particular immune-response problems at the doses needed for efficacy. Finally, they tried this idea out in a CFTR R553X mouse model to see if the sup-tRNA species could indeed rescue function in organoid tissues from these animals. I am glad to report that this worked! And it seems that combining this tRNA therapy with the existing CFTR drug combo (Trikafta) worked substantially better than either therapy alone - the authors believe, reasonably, that the tRNA allows for restored expression of the CFTR protein, while the modulator drug combo allows for its folding and trafficking to the membrane. So overall this is a real advance in getting tRNA therapy to work. There’s obviously going to be a lot more experimentation to do, and the range of things tried in this paper just serves to illustrate that. But this could turn out to be a real alternative for the many diseases for which gene therapy has been considered. It’s going to be quite a while before we run out of interesting things to do with RNA. . .
